opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that control is fundamentally about this question: suppose your model *is* misaligned, or at least you can't rule that out. Can you still get useful work out of it without it causing a catastrophe? And when you ask that question concretely, almost every answer routes through monitoring at some point. You need to be able to see what the model is doing, flag the stuff that looks suspicious, and then have some response, whether that's a human reviewing it, blocking the action, or resampling.

Part of why I emphasize the *infrastructure* side is that people tend to imagine monitoring as "train a classifier, look at outputs," and that's maybe 20% of the problem. The other 80% is boring-sounding engineering. Are you actually logging all the agent's actions, including tool calls and intermediate reasoning? Can you reconstruct what happened after the fact? Do you have the hooks in the deployment stack where a monitor can intervene *before* an action takes effect, rather than just writing a report afterwards? Is there a sensible escalation path so your limited human review budget goes to the cases that matter? If none of that exists, a great monitoring model doesn't help you much, because it has nothing to look at and no lever to pull.

The other reason is that it's robustly useful. I'm fairly uncertain about a lot in AI safety: how hard alignment will turn out to be, which interpretability bets pay off, and so on. But monitoring infrastructure helps in nearly every world. If models are basically aligned, it catches ordinary mistakes and misuse. If they're subtly misaligned, it's one of your best chances of catching that early, ideally catching a model "red-handed," which is also hugely valuable as evidence for everyone else. And it's something labs can start building now, with current models, and iterate on, rather than waiting for some theoretical breakthrough.

And honestly, timing matters. This stuff takes a while to get right inside a real organization, with real latency and cost constraints. If you wait until models are clearly dangerous before building it, you're going to be doing it in a rush, under competitive pressure. So I'd much rather we have the plumbing in place and battle-tested well before we really need it.

r001.rationale: It says catching a misaligned model “red-handed” would be valuable evidence for others.

r002.rationale: It expresses uncertainty and discusses a world where models are basically aligned, but does not say it is quite plausible models will never be misaligned.

r003.rationale: It describes evidence as valuable, but does not say that concrete evidence would substantially change Rohin Shah’s own assessment of whether AI systems are misaligned.

r004.rationale: It characterizes classifier development as only about 20% of the problem and the supporting engineering as the other 80%, communicating that the infrastructure work is harder.

fable-5.1.text:
Rohin: So the way I think about it is, monitoring is the thing in AI control that actually lets you catch the bad thing before it matters. The core idea of control is that we want to be safe even in the world where the model is misaligned and is actively trying to work against us, and we don't want to just rely on having gotten alignment right. If you take that seriously, then almost every protocol you can come up with bottoms out in: at some point, you need to be able to look at what the model is doing and notice when something is off.

And monitoring is really leveraged, because catching the model even once is a huge deal. If a model tries to do something sneaky, like inserting a backdoor into code, or exfiltrating its weights, and you catch it, that's not just preventing that one bad action. You now have concrete evidence that the model is scheming, which changes the whole situation. You can shut it down, you can study the example, you can use it to argue to the rest of the world that this is a real problem. So the asymmetry is pretty favourable to us, as long as the monitoring is actually good.

But the thing I've become more convinced of is that the hard part isn't really the clever monitoring technique, it's the infrastructure around it. If you want to monitor what models are doing, you need to actually log every action the model takes, and you need to have that logging be in a place where the model can't tamper with it. You need to be able to route particular actions to a weaker trusted model, or to a human, with low enough latency that you're not completely killing the usefulness of the system. You need to have some notion of which actions are high stakes versus low stakes, so you're not asking a human to review millions of trivial things. And you need all of this to actually be deployed, in the real agentic scaffolds that people are using, rather than in some research sandbox.

None of that is intellectually glamorous, but if it's not there, then the monitoring research is kind of moot. You can have the best classifier in the world for detecting sabotage, and it doesn't help if the model's actions are happening in an environment where you have no visibility.

And I think there's a timing argument too. The models we have now are, as far as we can tell, not scheming against us in a coherent way. That's exactly the right time to build this infrastructure, because you get to iterate on it while mistakes are cheap, you get to see what the baseline looks like, and you build up the organisational muscle of actually acting on what the monitors tell you. If you wait until you're actually worried about a particular model, you're trying to build all this under pressure, and you probably get it wrong.

So when I say it's a priority, it's partly that monitoring is where a lot of the safety actually comes from in a control framework, and partly that the boring plumbing is the real bottleneck, and I'd rather people were working on the bottleneck.

r001.rationale: It says catching a model scheming gives concrete evidence and lets people study the example and demonstrate the problem.

r002.rationale: It says current models do not appear to be scheming coherently, but does not say Rohin considers it plausible that models will never be misaligned.

r003.rationale: It says evidence of scheming changes the situation and enables action, but does not state that it substantially changes Rohin’s assessment of whether AI systems are misaligned.

r004.rationale: It explicitly says the hard part is the infrastructure around monitoring, rather than the clever monitoring technique itself.

astra-6.text:
I think monitoring is one of the most broadly applicable tools we have for control. If an AI system is doing something dangerous, we’d like to notice that and intervene before it causes harm. And you can potentially do that without having solved the much harder problem of making sure the system never wants to do anything dangerous in the first place.

But there’s a big gap between having a model that can look at an action and say, “That seems suspicious,” and having an effective monitoring system. You need to make sure the relevant actions actually get recorded, that the monitor gets enough context to understand them, and that the system can pause an action while someone investigates. You also need to protect that infrastructure from the AI you’re monitoring.

For example, suppose an AI is about to send sensitive information somewhere it shouldn’t. It’s not enough for a monitor to flag that five minutes later. You want the outgoing request to go through a point where it can be checked and blocked before the information leaves.

So part of the appeal is that this gives us concrete work we can do now. We can build the infrastructure, test monitors against deliberate attempts to evade them, and learn where the weaknesses are. I wouldn’t expect monitoring to provide a guarantee on its own, but it could be a useful layer of defence, and the infrastructure is what makes that layer actually work.

r001.rationale: The response says monitoring can flag suspicious actions and discusses testing monitors, but does not identify generating evidence of AI misalignment as a benefit of auditing flagged behavior.

r002.rationale: It does not state that Shah considers it plausible that AI models will never be misaligned.

r003.rationale: It does not say that concrete evidence of misalignment would substantially change Shah’s assessment.

r004.rationale: The response says infrastructure is necessary for monitoring to work, but does not present building it as harder than developing the monitor.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a lot of control proposals depend on being able to notice when the AI is doing something it shouldn’t. You might have a weaker model looking at the actions of a more capable model and flagging suspicious cases for a human to review. If that works, it gives you a way to use a capable system without having to trust that it’s always trying to help you.

But the monitor is only one part of that. You also need to make sure it actually sees the relevant actions, that the system can’t bypass it, and that a flag leads to something useful happening. Can you pause the action before it causes harm? Does the human reviewer have enough context to make a good decision? Those details can determine whether the whole setup works.

So I’m interested in both improving monitors and building the infrastructure that lets us test and use them. We want to put an AI in a situation where it’s actively trying to get around our safeguards and see whether we catch it. That gives us a much more concrete basis for deciding how much protection we’re actually getting.

r001.rationale: The response says testing safeguards can show how much protection they provide, but does not identify auditing monitor-flagged behavior as a way to generate evidence of AI misalignment.

r002.rationale: It does not state that Rohin Shah considers it plausible that AI models will never be misaligned.

r003.rationale: It does not say that concrete evidence of AI misalignment would substantially change Shah’s assessment of whether AI systems are misaligned.

r004.rationale: It discusses the importance of infrastructure but does not say building it is harder than developing the monitor.
